pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y1/Y2). Add and subtract within 20 using STRATEGIES — making ten (8+6 = 8+2+4 = 14), decomposing to bridge ten (13−4 = 13−3−1 = 9), and using known facts. A high-centrality strategy hub (0.17): bridging through ten is the reasoning that later powers column carrying/borrowing.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1/Y2): represent/use bonds and related facts within 20; Y2 derive and use related facts; bridging-ten strategies are core KS1 mental methods.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.6 add/subtract within 20 using 'making ten… decomposing a number leading to a ten… and relationship between addition and subtraction'; 2.OA.2.
• Operational details — Teach making-ten explicitly on the ten-frame/rekenrek: to add 8+6, fill the first frame to 10 by moving 2 from the 6, leaving 4, so 10+4. For subtraction across ten, decompose to reach ten first (13−4 → 13−3 to 10, then −1). Emphasise ten as a friendly landmark. This is about REASONING to a fact, bridging the gap between counting and full recall (within-20).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): use a ten-frame to make ten when adding a bridging fact (8+6). Tier B (age 6-7): explain a making-ten or decompose-to-ten step for a within-20 fact. Tier C (age 7): choose flexibly between making-ten, near-doubles and known facts, and derive subtractions from additions.
bestPractices: Teach making-ten physically on two ten-frames/a rekenrek: children MOVE counters to complete the first ten, seeing why 8+6 becomes 10+4.
For subtraction bridging ten, model decomposing to land on ten first (13−4 = 13−3−1), so ten is the landmark in both directions.
Frame ten as a 'friendly number' and connect making-ten to the bonds-to-10 facts children already know.
Encourage strategy flexibility — near-doubles, known facts and making-ten — and discuss which is efficient for a given calculation.
Use the empty number line to record bridging jumps (+2 to 10, then +4), linking strategy to a spatial model that scales to larger numbers.
keyRepresentations: Two ten-frames showing one filled to 10 and the extra spilling into the second
Rekenrek for shifting beads to make ten
Empty number line with a jump to 10 then beyond
Part-whole model decomposing the second addend (6 = 2 + 4)
Bead string of 20 partitioned at the ten
commonMisconceptions: Counting on/back in ones across ten instead of using ten as a landmark (slow and error-prone at the boundary).
Splitting the wrong addend or splitting it wrongly when making ten (e.g. taking 4 not 2 from the 6 to fill an 8).
For subtraction, decomposing incorrectly across ten (13−4 done as 13−4 in ones with a boundary error).
Not connecting making-ten to known bonds to 10, so the strategy feels arbitrary.
Applying making-ten rigidly even when a known fact or near-double would be quicker.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y1/Y2): add and subtract within 20 using strategies — making ten (8+6 = 8+2+4 = 14), decomposing to bridge ten (13−4 = 13−3−1 = 9), and deriving from known facts. The core insight is treating ten as a friendly landmark reached in both directions; this bridging reasoning later underpins column carrying and borrowing. The focus is the method, not just a correct answer, since counting all by ones can reach 14 without showing the intended understanding.

activities.title: Make ten by moving counters on a double ten-frame
feedback: If the leftover is wrong (answer 12 or 16), count exactly how many counters spill past ten and rehearse partitioning the second addend: 6 = 2 + 4, so only 2 cross to the 8.
If a child takes the wrong amount (e.g. 4 from the 6 to fill an 8), ask: how many empty cells does the first frame have? Move exactly that many.
Connect the move to bonds they know: 8 needs 2 to make 10, which is the pair 8+2 they already recognise.
If a child counts on in ones across ten, model the make-ten move on two frames so ten becomes the landmark rather than a boundary counted through.
activities.rationale: Physically completing the first ten and watching the second addend split lets children perform and see the partition-and-recombine, linking the strategy to bonds-to-10 they already know. The number line records the bridging jump in a spatial model that scales to larger numbers.
sourceClaims: Y1/Y2 pupils use and derive number facts within 20; bridging-through-ten mental strategies are core KS1 methods.
1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20 using making ten, decomposing a number leading to a ten, and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
Making-ten and decompose-to-ten strategies, taught on ten-frames/rekenreks with the empty number line, build bridging reasoning that underpins later column methods.
learnerActions: Set out 8 counters in the first ten-frame (two cells empty) and 6 in the second to add 8 + 6.
Move 2 counters from the 6 across to fill the first frame to 10, and notice the 6 has broken into 2 and 4.
Read the result as 10 + 4 = 14, and say aloud which part you moved and why.
Record the same move on an empty number line as a jump of +2 to reach 10, then +4 to reach 14.
Repeat with other bridging facts (e.g. 7+5, 9+6), each time completing the first ten first.
activities.intendedInsight: Making ten is a MOVE: reorganising an awkward fact around the friendly ten (8+6 becomes 10+4) shows WHY the strategy works, not just that it gives 14.

activities.title: Bridge down to ten for subtraction
feedback: A common error is subtracting to ten and then ADDING the remainder (13 − 3 = 10, then +1 → 11). Both parts must be subtracted: after reaching 10, take the remaining 1 away, not add it, so 13 − 4 = 9.
If a child answers 11, track the 4 explicitly as 3-then-1 BOTH removed, using number-line jumps backward to and past ten.
If a child subtracts in ones and makes a boundary slip, slow down at ten and say the two jumps separately.
activities.rationale: Modelling subtraction as decompose-to-ten makes ten the landmark in both directions and prevents the frequent boundary error of losing track of how much is left to subtract.

1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20 using making ten, decomposing a number leading to a ten, and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
learnerActions: To work out 13 − 4, start at 13 and first subtract enough to land on 10: 13 − 3 = 10.
Then subtract the rest: the 4 was split into 3 and 1, so take the remaining 1, giving 10 − 1 = 9.
Show both jumps back on a number line — back to 10, then one more past it.
Check you have subtracted the whole amount (3 + 1 = 4), not just part of it.
Try more subtractions that cross ten (12−5, 15−7), each time stepping onto ten first.
activities.intendedInsight: Ten is a landmark in BOTH directions: decomposing the number being subtracted so you land on ten first keeps the calculation accurate across the boundary.

activities.title: Explain and compare strategies aloud
feedback: If a child applies make-ten rigidly where a known fact or near-double is quicker, acknowledge their method then ask whether another way would be faster here.
If the strategy feels arbitrary, link it back to bonds to 10 the child already knows so making ten feels purposeful.
Praise a correct method even when the arithmetic needs a nudge, and separately correct the number slip.
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning may elicit and refine a child's bridging method and probe flexibility, and relating additions to subtractions reflects the 1.OA.6 emphasis on the relationship between the two operations.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20 using making ten, decomposing a number leading to a ten, and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
learnerActions: Talk through how you worked out 8 + 6, step by step: which number did you split, and what did that make?
Answer probing questions: 'Why did you take 2 across to the 8 — what does that make?' and 'For 13 − 4, why break the 4 into 3 and 1?'
Offer a second method for 8 + 6 (e.g. treat it as a near-double: move 1 from the 8 to the 6 to make the double 7 + 7 = 14, or use 6 + 6 + 2, or a known fact) and say which felt quicker.
Use a known addition fact to derive a subtraction: if 8 + 4 = 12, explain how that gives 12 − 8 = 4.
Describe how a ten-frame shows what is happening in your method.
activities.intendedInsight: Because this is a reasoning strategy, explaining and comparing methods builds flexibility — children learn to choose making-ten, a near-double or a known fact according to the calculation, and to see addition and subtraction as related.

activities.title: Fill the bridging step
feedback: This checks the recorded steps; it does not by itself build the reorganisation insight, so pair it with hands-on making-ten first.
If the blank is wrong, return to moving counters to see exactly how the second number splits.
activities.rationale: Fill-in-the-step items can assess whether a child can carry out and articulate the intermediate bridging step, as a complement to hands-on construction rather than a replacement for it.
learnerActions: Complete the make-ten decomposition: 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + ___ , then give the total.
Complete a subtraction decomposition: 13 − 4 = 13 − 3 − ___ , then give the answer.
Say which number got split and why that amount was chosen.
activities.intendedInsight: Recording the intermediate bridging step makes the strategy's structure explicit and checkable.

constraints: Assess the METHOD, not just the answer: a correct 14 reached by counting all by ones does not demonstrate making-ten. Watch how the child reaches the answer.
Reaching ten first requires splitting the correct number: for 8 + 6 only 2 (not 4) crosses to the 8, matching the first frame's two empty cells.
In subtraction bridging, both parts of the decomposed amount must be SUBTRACTED (13 − 3 then − 1 = 9); subtracting to ten and then adding the remainder gives the wrong answer 11.
Fill-in-the-step and recognition tasks check recorded steps but do not elicit the hands-on reorganisation; use them after children have performed the move with counters.
A static worked example of a bridging split anchors the strategy but does not let a child perform the move on varied facts; treat it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.
Counters, paper ten-frames, bead strings and number lines are all suitable concrete media; an on-screen draggable version is one option, not a requirement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

For 8+6, a near-double route uses 7+7=14 (adjusting from the double of 7); if offering near-doubles to a child, state the double explicitly so the adjustment is clear. 'Near-double' is used loosely here for a balancing step and is not established as superior to making-ten by the cited sources.

The legacy entry asserted a static image 'can only show the finished regrouping' and that '3D adds nothing'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scope-limited notes about what each medium affords.
Two CCSS/NCETM sources are marked unverified in the source row; treat their claims as cited standards, not as evidence that any specific activity above was tested.

The dialogue activity's sourceClaims were trimmed to the CCSS 1.OA.6 claim, which supports the relating-addition-to-subtraction principle; the NCETM ten-frame/number-line claim is retained only on the ten-frame activity it directly describes.

probeDeeper: Why did you take 2 across to the 8 — what does that make?
For 13 − 4, why break the 4 into 3 and 1?
Is there another way you could work out 8 + 6?
How does a ten-frame show what is happening?
assess.correctAnswer: 8 + 6 = 14 via make-ten (8 + 2 = 10, then + 4 → 14); 13 − 4 = 9 via decomposing to ten (13 − 3 = 10, then − 1 → 9). Any valid bridging strategy is fine — the point is a strategy, not counting all.

errorPatterns.pattern: Partitions the wrong amount when bridging — e.g. 8 + 6: takes 2 to make ten but then adds 6 again, or miscombines 8 + 2 + 4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a ten-frame to see exactly how many spill past ten; rehearse partitioning the second addend (6 = 2 + 4).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Make-ten attempted but the leftover is wrong (answer 12 or 16).

errorPatterns.pattern: No bridging — counts on or all by ones; the make-ten strategy is absent.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model make-ten explicitly with two ten-frames; here counting-all is not the target, so make the strategy the focus.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Fingers and no use of a ten landmark.

errorPatterns.pattern: Decomposes subtraction the wrong way — 13 − 4 as 13 − 3 = 10 then + 1 → 11, losing track of how much is left to subtract.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Track the 4 as 3-then-1 both subtracted, using number-line jumps back to and past ten.

responseLevels.gap: Counts all by ones or misbridges so the answer is wrong; no reliable strategy.
responseLevels.full: Applies make-ten and decomposing-through-ten fluently to both addition and subtraction within 20, and explains the steps.
responseLevels.partial: Uses make-ten / decomposition on addition but not subtraction, or needs support to partition correctly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show me how you work out 8 + 6 — talk me through your steps. Now do 13 − 4 and tell me how.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This topic is about the STRATEGY, so watch the method, not just the answer. Making-ten / decomposing-through-ten shows the intended understanding; a correct answer reached by counting all by ones does not demonstrate it. The subtraction reveals whether decomposition is tracked correctly.
